name: Sunekos

lead: Sunekos is an injectable that combines hyaluronic acid with amino acids, offered in clinics for photoaged face skin, the eye area and lax skin on the thighs, knees and arms. People use it for firmer, less crepey skin.

The idea is that the amino acids supply building blocks for collagen and elastin and support fibroblast activity, so skin tissue is stimulated. Published work includes a multicenter cellulite study of 46 women, and registered small studies cover the face, under-eyes and body.

paras: A clinician injects the mixture into or beneath the dermis at several points over the area being treated, typically across a short course of sessions. It is used on the face, around the eyes and on body skin.
The cellulite study assessed safety alongside efficacy. As with other injectables, local swelling and bruising are expected, and long-term safety data are limited.

angle.text: Sunekos is an Italian biorevitalising booster that combines hyaluronic acid and amino acids, used for firmer skin on photoaged faces, around the eyes and on lax areas like the thighs and arms. The amino acids are meant to supply building blocks for collagen and elastin. Support is mainly small manufacturer-linked trials.

lead: Sunekos is a commercially available mixture of hyaluronic acid and amino acids in an alkaline solution, injected for skin aesthetics.[1] Registered studies have evaluated it for face photoaging, the area around the eyes and skin laxity of the inner thighs, knees and arms.[2][3][4][5]
A 2026 prospective multicenter study evaluated the mixture for cellulite (edematous fibrosclerotic panniculopathy) in 46 women using an injection technique, reporting on efficacy and safety.[1]
infobox: Hyaluronic acid plus amino acid injectable

Face, under-eyes, inner thighs, knees, arms, cellulite

paras: The 2026 cellulite study was prospective and multicenter, enrolling 46 women with stage I to early stage disease and assessing both efficacy and safety.[1]

Registered studies include a twelve-person half-face comparison of two injection techniques for photoaging,[2] a 25-person intradermal photoaging study,[5] a 22-person under-eye dark circle study,[4] and a 24-person study on inner thighs, knees and arms.[3] Posted results were not available in the sources reviewed.
